name: Anna
title: The Prophetess in the Temple
lifespan: About 84 years old, or possibly over 100, at Jesus' presentation in the temple
summary: When the promised child was brought into the temple in Jerusalem, an elderly prophetess stood ready to receive him. Anna, the daughter of Phanuel from the tribe of Asher, had spent decades in uninterrupted prayer and fasting after becoming a widow just seven years into her marriage. Luke paints a picture of a woman whose entire life was directed toward God in expectation. As Simeon completed his prophecy over the child Jesus, Anna stepped forward, praised God, and proclaimed to all who were waiting for Jerusalem’s redemption that God’s promises were now being fulfilled. That she belonged to the tribe of Asher—counted among the northern tribes lost after the Assyrian exile—underscores that God had preserved a faithful remnant from all His people. Together, Simeon and Anna form two witnesses, man and woman, confirming that God’s salvation has now broken into history. Anna’s life story shows that long, faithful waiting on God is not in vain: those who endure in prayer will ultimately see the fulfillment of what God has promised.

keyEvents.title: Anna's Background and Faithful Temple Service
keyEvents.description: Anna was the daughter of Penuel from the tribe of Asher. She had been married for seven years before becoming a widow, and was now very old. She never left the temple but served God with fasting and prayer night and day through many long years.

keyEvents.title: Jesus' Presentation in the Temple – The Setting for Anna's Testimony
keyEvents.description: According to the Law of Moses, Jesus was brought to the temple in Jerusalem to be presented to the Lord. It was on this occasion – when the purification offering was brought and the child was dedicated – that Anna saw the promised child.

keyEvents.title: Simeon's prophecy as a precursor to Anna's testimony
keyEvents.description: Just before Anna came forward, the elderly Simeon had taken the infant Jesus in his arms and prophesied about him. He told Mary that the child was set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and that a sword would pierce her own soul. Anna's testimony followed immediately after and confirmed Simeon's prophetic words.

keyEvents.title: Anna recognizes the infant Jesus and testifies to redemption
keyEvents.description: At the very moment Simeon prophesied, Anna came forward and praised God. She spoke about the infant Jesus to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. Her testimony makes her one of the very first to proclaim the coming of the Messiah.

keyEvents.title: Anna as a representative of the tribe of Asher and all Israel
keyEvents.description: Anna belonged to the tribe of Asher, one of the ten northern tribes that many considered lost after the Assyrian exile in 722 BC. Her presence in the temple and her prophetic testimony show that God still had faithful worshippers from all the tribes of Israel, and that his promises applied to the entire people.

versions.summary: Anna was an elderly prophetess from the tribe of Asher who served God in the temple in Jerusalem with fasting and prayer day and night. She was among the first to recognize the newborn infant Jesus as the Messiah when he was brought to the temple. Together with the elderly Simeon, she testified about the child's significance for Israel's redemption.
versions.title: The Prophetess in the Temple
versions.reason: [minor] The title is precise and descriptive, but could optionally clarify that she was a widow, as this is a central part of her identity in the text. The current title is still good.; [major] Anna is described in Luke 2:36–38 as one who served God with fasting and prayer night and day, and she testified about the child to all who were waiting for redemption. She should also have the roles 'widow' and 'worshiper' in addition to 'prophet,' since these are central to her biblical characterization.; [minor] The text in Luke 2:36–37 can be understood in two ways: either she was 84 years old, or she had been a widow for 84 years (which would make her over 100). The current wording follows the most common interpretation, but this should be mentioned in a footnote.; [minor] Event 4 ('Simeon's prophecy as context for Anna's testimony') deals primarily with Simeon, not with Anna. Although it provides useful context, the description should be more clearly linked to Anna's perspective, or considered shortened since it is actually another person's event.; [minor] Event 6 ('Anna testifies about redemption') overlaps significantly with Event 2 ('Anna recognizes the child Jesus'), as both concern Luke 2:38. These could usefully be combined to avoid repetition.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. A profile should include footnotes covering interesting historical, linguistic, and theological details, for example about the meaning of Anna's name, the tribe of Asher after the exile, and the double interpretation of her age.

versions.summary: Anna was an elderly prophetess from the tribe of Asher who served God in the temple in Jerusalem with fasting and prayer day and night. She was the daughter of Phanuel and had been married for seven years before she became a widow. At Jesus' presentation in the temple, she was among the first to recognize the newborn child as the Messiah. Together with the old man Simeon, she testified about the significance of the child, and she spoke about him to all who were waiting for Jerusalem's redemption. Anna represents God's faithful remnant among all the tribes of Israel and stands in the tradition of female prophets in the Bible.
versions.title: The Prophetess in the Temple
versions.reason: [minor] The lifetime description is somewhat imprecise. The Greek text allows two interpretations (84 years old or a widow for 84 years), which has already been noted in the footnotes. It may be useful to reflect this ambiguity directly in the lifespan field.; [minor] The summary is good but closely resembles the previous version (version 1). It should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from earlier versions and add greater depth—for example, by highlighting the theological significance of her testimony and her role as one of two witnesses at Jesus' presentation.; [minor] The event "Jesus' presentation in the temple" concerns context more than Anna herself. While it is acceptable to include as background, it should be made clearer that this forms the framework for Anna's experience.; [minor] The account of Simeon's prophecy provides important context, but the many verses (25–32) focus primarily on Simeon rather than Anna. versions.summary: Anna, daughter of Phanuel from the tribe of Asher, was a prophetess who had devoted most of her life to prayer and fasting in the temple in Jerusalem. After only seven years of marriage she became a widow and spent the rest of her days in unceasing worship and service to God. When Mary and Joseph brought the child Jesus to the temple to present him to the Lord, Anna stepped forward as a prophetic witness alongside the elderly Simeon. She praised God and proclaimed to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem that this child was the fulfillment of God's promises. As one belonging to the tribe of Asher – one of the northern tribes many considered lost after the Assyrian exile – Anna testifies that God preserved a faithful remnant from all Israel. Luke's account of her emphasizes that God's work of salvation was confirmed through two witnesses, a man and a woman, and that even those who had waited their whole lives saw God's promises come to pass.

To distinguish itself more from earlier versions and add freshness, the introduction should be rephrased and the perspective adjusted somewhat.; [minor] The event 'Jesus' Presentation in the Temple – the framework for Anna's testimony' provides relevant context but focuses primarily on Jesus and his parents rather than directly on Anna. This, however, is a matter of judgment.

footnotes.text: The name "Anna" (Greek: Ἅννα, Hanna) means "grace" or "favor" in Hebrew, and is the same name as the prophet Samuel's mother in the Old Testament (1 Sam 1). This name similarity may have theological resonance, since both women are connected to the temple context and God's plan of salvation.

The tribe of Asher was one of the ten northern tribes that were taken away in the Assyrian exile in 722 BC. The fact that Anna is identified as belonging to this tribe shows that some from the so-called "lost tribes" still maintained their tribal identity and lived in the Jewish heartland. This has theological significance as a sign of God's faithfulness to all Israel.

The Greek text in Luke 2:37 can be interpreted in two ways: either Anna was 84 years old, or she had been a widow for 84 years. If she married around the age of 14 and was married for 7 years, the latter interpretation would make her about 105 years old. Both interpretations emphasize her long-lasting faithfulness and service in the temple.

Anna's practice of fasting and prayer "night and day" in the temple reflects a form of temple asceticism known from Jewish tradition. Although women did not have formal service in the temple, devout widows could spend much time in the temple area, especially in the Court of Women. Her prophetic gift places her in a tradition of female prophets in the Old Testament, such as Miriam, Deborah, and Huldah.

The fact that Luke highlights two witnesses – Simeon and Anna – at Jesus' presentation in the temple may reflect the biblical principle that a matter must be confirmed by the mouth of two witnesses (Deut 19:15). The fact that one witness is a man and the other a woman underscores the universality of God's message of salvation.

In rabbinic tradition, old age was often seen as a sign of God's blessing and as a reward for a righteous life. Anna's advanced age and uninterrupted temple service would have given her considerable spiritual authority in the contemporary Jewish context, which strengthens the credibility and weight of her prophetic testimony about the infant Jesus.

Luke is the only evangelist who tells about Anna. His gospel has a clear tendency to highlight women and their role in salvation history—from Elizabeth and Mary to the women at the tomb. Including Anna as a prophetic witness fits into this broader pattern.
